title: Lets Take a Look at D6: Dungeons, Dudes, Dames, Danger, Dice and Dragons
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0_ptJC7W48

Daniel (@dungeondive) returns to D6: Dungeons, Dudes, Dames, Danger, Dice and Dragons from Certifiable Studios, a game that was on his most-anticipated list two years earlier. It confirms his suspicion that the solo mode can't carry it. This is a light, beer-and-pretzels competitive game, and that's where its mojo lives.

He praises the production at length. The double-sided board is drawn as a GM's annotated map, and there are wooden stat tokens, metal coins, signposts that carry rules, and around 40 chibi-style standees he'd happily keep for other games. The highlight is the GM Events section, a d100 table of well-written random events (he reads the ogre that falls on a child in full), backed by d8, d10 and d12 lists for nearly 150 events in all.

The rulebook is where it falls apart. The handsome hardback recommends using the rules on the website instead. Character backgrounds are in the book, but no names appear on the cards. Stealth comes straight after setup, before how to take a turn, and "discard" and "equip" never appear. He recounts the designers' own playthrough stalling when neither could find a rule in their book. The take-that heroic quest deck, the game's most creative part, isn't used solo at all. Shelf space decides it: the game goes to the sell pile.

----

Daniel's verdict: a gorgeous game whose rulebook tells you to go online. How much does a rulebook's quality weigh in whether you keep a game?
